newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Japan, New Zealand break ranks with UK on Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Japan, New Zealand break ranks with UK on Hong Kong.

text.p: Japan and New Zealand broke ranks with Britain on Friday by refusing to join a boycott of the swearing-in of Hong Kong's new China-appointed legislature during the handover ceremonies in 18 days.

Frequent Sino-British disputes have marred much of Hong Kong's drawn out 13-year transition to Chinese rule, which began when the two nations signed a handover treaty in 1984 without regard to the wishes of the territory's six million people.

So British Prime Minister Tony Blair's decision to boycott the latter half of the grand handover ceremony, when Beijing will inaugurate an unelected, post-handover legislature, is stirring concerns that the end of 156 years of British rule will be remembered for the wrong reason.
China's demand on Thursday to march the troops of the future garrison into Hong Kong ahead of the midnight handover is likely to fuel the tension, politicians and diplomats said.
Pro-democracy activist Christine Loh accused China of seeking to move the goalposts and argued it was a worrying sign of things to come.
China had earlier agreed to limit its pre-handover military presence to just a small, unarmed advance party which is already in place.
"We don't want to see a pattern of China wanting to negotiate and then re-negotiate and re-re-negotiate," Loh said.
Washington has backed the British stance and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will shun the investiture ceremony.

But New Zealand's Foreign Minister Don McKinnon told parliament that Wellington had already made known its opposition to China's decision to dissolve the present elected Legislative Council and saw no point in a boycott.
"I see no point in carrying on a higher level of antagonism," McKinnon said.
Japan, whose often rocky relations with China have thawed in recent months, also announced officials would attend the swearing-in.
"I know there is an issue over whether we should go to this or not," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters. "But I think we must go."

More than 4,000 guests invited by Britain and China are expected to witness the extravagant joint handover ceremony marking the end of Britain's imperial adventures in Asia and what China regards as a century and a half of humiliation.

But Beijing's plan to install the chamber promptly after the flag change, in the presence of the international dignitaries, put Blair and VIPs from other countries that contest the legitimacy of the provisional legislature in a diplomatic bind.

In Hong Kong, leader of the popular Democratic Party Martin Lee said he was disappointed that Japan and New Zealand should decide to send their top officials to attend the swearing-in ceremony of members of a chamber, which they did not support.
"I am disappointed that these governments should on one hand say this should not have been done, and on the other hand, they attend the swearing in ceremony," Lee told Reuters.
"It's a confusing message," he said.

Australia on Thursday dashed British hopes of a unified Western stand by putting national interest first and declining to join the United States and Britain in shunning the post-midnight investiture ceremony.
Other nations have yet to indicate what they will do.
A Hong Kong government spokesman said it was up to individual countries to whether to attend a ceremony marking the striking down of an elected legislature.
"It's up to elected politicians to explain to their own constituents how they reached their decision," he added.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook sought to pour oil on the troubled waters on Friday by declaring Hong Kong should serve as a bridge, not a barrier, between London and Beijing.
Cook, who will attend the ceremonies along with Blair, said: "Hong Kong should be a bridge, not a barrier, between Britain and China."
But he also pledged Britain would monitor events in the territory beyond the handover, a plan that has made China bristle and protest about interference in internal affairs.
"We have agreed to report to parliament every six months on Hong Kong at least until the turn of the century," Cook wrote in the London Times.
Hong Kong's democratic lobby, which has denounced the provisional legislature as a travesty of democracy, have welcomed Britain's monitoring plans.
But they have expressed disappointment that London has not sued Beijing in the International Court of Justice on the grounds of breaching the terms of the 1984 handover treaty.

The 1984 Joint Declaration set the June 30 handover date and also bound China to leaving Hong Kong alone to run its own affairs and to refraining from imposing communism on the fiercely capitalist community for 50 years.

But China, infuriated by mild last minute democratic reforms instigated by outgoing British Governor Chris Patten, will reverse them when it dissolves the Legislative Council returned in 1995 by one million voters.
In its place goes the Provisional Legislature, a 60-member chamber chosen by a hand-picked panel of 400 pro-Beijing worthies in Hong Kong.
Pro-democracy activists view the provisional assembly as the beginning of a more authoritarian style of rule.

One of Tung's aides denied there were any plans to clip freedoms. "The (future) Hong Kong governemnt knows, and it understands that freedom is very close to our hearts... So we are determined that we will enjoy no less freedom after 1997 than we have before," Nellie Fung, a member of Tung's inner cabinet, told reporters.
